blocks.p: In the thirtieth year of his marriage, Sol could no longer climb the counting-house stair without stopping on the landing to breathe, and Lyda had given up pretending that she did not wait for him at the top.

She stood there most mornings with the day’s first manifest under her arm and never offered to help, and he loved her for it. When he reached the top she handed it to him, as if that were what she had been waiting for, and went in ahead of him.

Philippa’s heavy pull was hard on old knees. He was eighty-two by Lucan’s reckoning, which Lucan had kept up faithfully, calipers and all, until the winter he died. Sol’s hair had gone from grey to white and then thinned almost to nothing, and the skin of his hands had loosened over the knuckles and taken on the brown spots, and when he held them still a faint tremor ran through them, as if something under the skin were trying to remember a tune. He still had the seizures, three or four a year now. He knew them coming by the smell of oranges, and lay down wherever he was, and woke with somebody’s coat under his head and somebody’s hand resting on the boards beside it. On the river every child over five knew how to do that. A good many of them had learned it on him.

Lyda was sixty-seven. Her hair was as white as his, cropped short as a boy’s, and her face had gone lean and fine, the bones coming up under it the way rock comes up through a hillside in a dry year. She still ran the line. The Thorne ships went now to worlds that had not been charted when Sol first came out of the cold on Philippa, and on half of them, in a loft or a seed house or the back room of a chandlery, a few people met around a copy of a copy of Stephen’s notebook, and baptized one another in whatever water there was, and buried their dead, and wept.

The longest letters, and the worst-spelled, came from Teo, who was forty-eight and browned by a dozen suns and still had his spells, and who had gone out that year to a new world called Colossa, past Ephes, where there were already nine people meeting in a dyer’s yard. They ask whether you were really the bishop, he wrote. I tell them you were.

Teo had Lucan’s ledgers now, forty-one of them bound in grey. The doctor had come to it very late, and by evidence, as he came to everything: twenty years at the end of the pier with Lyda, drawing lines through his objections one by one, until one spring there was nothing left to draw a line through, and he went down into the Wend at first light, a very old man, with Teo’s arm under his. He wept coming up out of the water, to his own astonishment, and afterward he wrote it down. They buried him four years later in the field above the dye works, under a stone Tobin had cut. Sol went up most evenings when his knees allowed and told him things. It seemed to him the doctor would have wanted the data.

Tobin was ninety, or near it, and no longer got up the hill. He sat in the afternoons in a chair at the end of the Thorne pier with a blanket over his knees, watching the ships come in, and when Sol came down the pier at the end of the day, Tobin would reach out without looking and take hold of his wrist, and hold it a while, and let it go.
The noise still came, not often, never for long, in his own voice, flattened and catching, with the crackle under it. Too late. Too old. Nothing on the other side. He said the name, and it broke.

Aurelian had never answered. Sol prayed for him every night by name. Some years he thought he was praying for a man who had gone under in the east hall and come up smooth and fond and amused, with a gap where a friend had been. Some years he thought he was praying for a man who had forgotten nothing.
And on the river, all that time, Ansel Weir kept the registry.

The hood parts had come in Lyda’s hold that first autumn, and Weir had gone under first, as she had promised him, and every time since. He knew, of course, who went down into the Wend at first light and came up dark. He wrote down every name, and the registry went up the line to Sion every quarter, and nothing ever came of it, because out here nothing could. The believers made a joke of it: Mind your hair, Weir’s got a slate.
He came along the wharf on a rain evening at the end of the dry season, walking faster than Sol had ever seen him walk, with another man beside him.

Sol saw them from the counting-house window: Weir with his slate over his head against the rain, and a taller man in a traveling cloak, hood up, moving with a long easy stride that did not belong to Philippa’s heavy pull. Something in Sol knew the walk before the rest of him did. He put the manifest down.
Weir brought the man to the foot of the stair, looked up, saw Sol in the lit window, and touched his temple, a small pleased gesture. Then he went away, quickly.
The man in the cloak put his hood back.
He had not changed.

Aurelian Croft stood in the lamplight on the Thorne wharf exactly as he had stood at the edge of Sol’s life for as long as Sol could remember: the silver hair worn long in the fashionable way, the fine bones, the face of a handsome man of about forty with a look of private amusement about the mouth, and the small worried crease between the brows, which had outlasted every cycle in the east hall. The rain ran off his face as it would have run off glass.

Sol went down, stopping on the landing to breathe, and all the way down Aurelian watched him come with the look of the crowd in the Bounty Market. His eyes went to the white hair and the spotted hands and the stoop, and something in the handsome face flinched and could not stop flinching.
Then Aurelian put out both hands, and took Sol’s, and turned them over in his own, and looked at them.
“Tarren,” he said. His voice was the same too. “You told me I mightn’t know your voice. You didn’t say anything about your face.”

They sat by the stove in the house across the yard, with the rain on the roof. Lyda put a cup of tea into Aurelian’s hands and sat down across from him with her own, and said nothing at all. He looked at the shelf where Lucan’s spectacles still lay, and at Lyda’s cropped white head, and most of all at Sol, and kept looking away and coming back.
“I came on the church packet,” he said. “Nobody stops a bishop. I told the Hierarch’s office I was making a visitation of the Diaspora chapels. I’ve visited one.”
“Weir’s,” Lyda said.

“Nobody reads the registries. I read his, Tarren. I know the names of your people better than I know my own clergy’s. I know who baptized whom, and who died, and when you were ill.” He did not look up. “I couldn’t ask anyone about you. I could read.”
“Why did you come?” Sol said.
Aurelian set the cup on the floor, carefully, as if he were afraid of it.

“I’ve gone into the sealed room a hundred times since that night,” he said. “I go in at the twenty-second hour and sit in front of the panel for the quarter hour, and I never once open the line, and then I get up and go to dinner. I’m at the Hierarch’s table three nights a week, making the jokes.” He drew a breath. “I need to tell you something. About the Petrel.”
Across the stove, Lyda’s cup stopped halfway to her mouth.

“You wrote from Viper that you didn’t know what I’d done, or whether I knew it, and you forgave me anyway. I’ve read that letter until the wax came off. I need you to know what it was you forgave. I asked for your road to be changed. I was told...” He stopped. He looked at Lyda, and at the rain on the window, and something went over his face too quickly for Sol to name. “There’s more. There’s something about now. I came all this way to...”
He stopped again. The crease between his brows had deepened until it looked like a cut.
“Aurelian,” Sol said gently.

“No. Afterward. I’ll tell you all of it afterward, I swear it. In the water, if you like.” His voice steadied. “That’s why I’m here. I want to go into the water. I’ve wanted it for thirty years and been too frightened to say so, and I’m still frightened, but I’m here. Will you do it for me?”
“There’s a river at the bottom of the yard,” Sol said.

“Not here.” Aurelian leaned forward. “I’ve been on your world four hours and I’m already thinking about the packet home. If I do it here, it’ll go soft on the crossing, and by the time I wake at Plenty it’ll be something that happened to someone else. I know myself. I can’t do it out here; I’ll lose my nerve.” His voice dropped. “Where Stephen died.”
“Serenity,” Sol said.

“There’s water under the ice. There’s an old intake hall below the Long Gallery where they bring the sea up, and a pool in it. I’ve been to look. Come as my guest. My pass, my packet from Plenty; no one questions a bishop’s guest. An afternoon on the ice, and you’re gone again, and I’ll be like you. They won’t be able to read me either.”
“And afterward,” Lyda said, “how does he get back out?”

Aurelian turned to her as if he had forgotten she was there, and then his face did something Sol had never seen it do in all the years he had known it. It went blank for half a breath, like a Window with nothing behind it.
“The way he came,” Aurelian said.
He slept in the loft above the old dye shed. Sol stood at the bedroom window and watched the lamp come on across the yard, and watched it stay on, long past the middle of the night.
“He’s lying,” Lyda said from the bed.
“Some of it.”
“Which part?”
“I don’t know. I don’t think he knows.”

“He came to my stair with Weir, Sol. Weir has been writing us down for thirty years, and he never once walked anybody to the foot of my stair.” She was quiet a moment. “Frightened men are the ones who do things. I said it the night you told him where you’d be in the spring.” She sat up. “And think about where he wants you. Out here they can’t touch you. The Mercy Office has no warrant past Plenty; you’ve told me so yourself. Out here all they can do is what they did at the Scatter, through somebody else’s hands, and hope it looks like weather. But Serenity is theirs. Set one foot on that ice and you’re a man with an Order of Mercy on him.”
“I know.”
“Then he isn’t asking you to baptize him. He’s asking you to come where you can be taken.”
“Perhaps he’s asking both. You were right then, Lyda. You’re right now.”
“Then why are you standing at that window like a man who’s going?”
He did not answer for a long time. The rain ran down the glass between him and the loft lamp.

“Stephen came to the market,” he said at last. “He knew what I’d sign when I found him, and where it would end. He came anyway. He said there was one person in all the worlds he owed it to.” He turned from the window. “Aurelian has asked me for the water. Whatever else he’s asking, he’s asked for that. I’ve never once refused it to anyone. I don’t know how to begin with him.”
She looked at him from the bed, sharp and tired and unimpressed. Then she threw the blanket back and got up and began, in her nightgown, to take things down from the shelf.
“What are you doing?”

“Packing. Where you go, I will go. I said it in front of forty people and Tobin, and I’m not taking it back because you’ve found a way to make it inconvenient.” She put his old travel case on the bed. “Lucan’s box has taken me through thirty crossings. Don’t argue. You’ll lose, and it’ll take all night, and you look a hundred.”
“Eighty-two.”
“Go to bed.”

In the morning, before the ship, he went down the pier to Tobin, and lowered himself onto the bollard beside the old man’s chair, and took the bundle out from under his coat and laid it in Tobin’s lap.

There were three things in the same cloth: the brown block of Stephen’s Bible, which no one had dared open in twenty years; the grey notebook, its spine gone white, its pages furred at the edges from thirty years of thumbs; and Stephen’s journal, the old relay ledger with its cracked cover mended in tape, which began Dear Stephen and ended Dear Sol. Tobin did not unwrap them. He knew them by the weight.
“For Teo,” Sol said. “When he comes home.”
“You’re not coming back.”
“I don’t know.”

“He didn’t either.” Tobin did not need to say who. “He went to the market anyway.” He reached out without looking and found Sol’s wrist and held it. Then he let go, and lifted his hand, heavily, and laid it on Sol’s white head.
“Brother,” he said. That was all.

They went out on the Linnet that afternoon, with Aurelian in the pod across the aisle. Sol lay down in the cold and felt the frost come over the glass in its white ferns, and waited for the noise. In thirty years of crossings it had never once missed the moment the lid came down.

It did not come. Not at Plenty, where they changed to the church packet under Aurelian’s pass; not in the long blue hold going down to Serenity. All the way in, out of the Diaspora and down into reach, there was nothing in Sol’s head but his own silence. He noticed it the way you notice a dog that does not bark.
They came into Serenity at the end of the night watch. Aurelian left them at a pilgrims’ lodging off the Long Gallery and went up to the church residence, and came back for them at noon.

Serenity had not changed. Nothing in the inner colonies changed; that was what they were for. The lanterns went away overhead along the Long Gallery, each with Jupiter at the top of it like an eye, and Lyda stopped under the first and looked up, and the light came down the shaft onto her white head and made her look carved.
“That’s a lot of sky to put in a well,” she said.

People looked. Every face here was smooth, and every one turned as the two of them passed, and a man by a fruit stall pulled his small son against his legs and turned the child’s face away. Aurelian walked ahead and did not look back.

The intake hall lay below the end of the gallery, down a stair cut in the ice that wound until the lamps ran out and there was only the blue of the ice itself, lit from somewhere inside. The pumps stood against the far wall, dull housings the height of a house, and their throb came up through the floor into Sol’s knees. In the middle of the hall, ringed by a low rail, was the pool. It went down through the ice into the sea, and a thin mist curled off it toward the roof, and under the mist the water was perfectly still and perfectly black. Sol had never seen water that looked so deep.

Aurelian went to the rail. He took off his cloak and folded it and laid it on the ice. Under it he wore a plain white shirt, open at the throat. He took off his shoes and set them beside the cloak, and stood barefoot in front of the black water, and turned around.
His face was wet. Sol thought at first it was the mist.
“I came down this morning,” Aurelian said. “I stood on the step, up to my knees. I stood there an hour, Tarren, and I couldn’t...” He stopped. “It’s very cold.”
“It’s always cold,” Sol said. “That isn’t what stops people.”
“No.” Aurelian came toward him across the ice. “No, it isn’t.”

He put his arms around Sol. He had to stoop to do it now. He held him the way he had held him on the steps of the east hall after every renewal since their ordination, one hand spread between Sol’s shoulder blades, and then he turned his head and kissed him once on the cheek, as brother bishops greeted one another in Sion. His lips were cold. He did not let go.
“Tell me something they took,” he whispered.

It was what he had said on those steps, every time, with the taste of the hood still in their mouths; and then each told the other some small thing the cycle had lifted out of him, and they said the response together and laughed. Sol had not heard it in thirty years. Nobody had taken anything from him in thirty years. But the old answer was there, worn smooth, and it came out of him before he could stop it, because it was his turn and because it was true.
“You were frightened,” he said into Aurelian’s shoulder.

He waited for it. Not anymore. Aurelian’s breath shook against his ear, and did not say it, and his arms tightened. “I’m sorry,” he whispered. “I’m so sorry. I meant it, Tarren. I swear to you I meant every word...”
Over his shoulder, from behind the housings of the pumps, the wardens came out.

There were six of them. They came across the blue ice in white, calm and kind, not hurrying, the way the Mercy Office had always come. The senior warden was a woman with a gentle face and folded hands, and she stopped a few paces off and waited, politely, for the bishop to finish.
Aurelian let go and stepped back. His face was not blank now. It was everything at once.

“Sol Tarren, formerly Bishop of Life.” The warden touched her temple and read from the corner of her sight. “Received into Mercy, for the blasphemies of the name and of mourning, to be brought to Sion for judgment. By the hand of Aurelian Croft, Bishop of Life.” She looked up. “Signed at Plenty, at the evening office, yesterday.”
“I had to,” Aurelian said. It was barely a voice. “You understand that I had to.”
“Yes,” Sol said. “I understand.”
The warden turned to Lyda. “And you are?”
“His wife.”
The warden’s face went blank for a moment, as if she had been handed a coin from some other world and did not know what it would buy, and then smoothed. “On a term?”
“For life,” Lyda said.
“Of course.” The warden smiled at her with great kindness, as at a foreigner. “You may come with him. We aren’t unkind.”
Two of them came to his sides, and one touched his elbow to turn him toward the stair, and he went. Lyda walked beside him with her hand on his arm and did not look back. Sol did.

Before the stair turned, he saw Aurelian one last time: a slim figure in a white shirt standing barefoot at the rail, alone, with his shoes set neatly beside him and the mist going up past him like breath on a cold morning. He had not gone in. He was looking down at the water.
He was still looking at it when the ice closed between them.
